Anthraquinones are laxatives

Several glycosides in which the Aglycones are Anthracene derivatives occur as the pharmacologically active constituents of several cathartics/stimulant laxatives of plant origin.

Forms of different oxidation-levels

The anthracene occur in these medicinal plants in various forms of different oxidation-levels as derivatives of :

(Anthraquinone, Anthrone, Oxanthrone or Anthranol, as well as in a dimeric forms (dianthrone) in some cases.

Slide 2 figure: Anthracene — three fused rings, positions numbered 1–10 (top row 1 · 9 · 8; sides 2, 3 and 7, 6; bottom row 4 · 10 · 5).

Derivatives of anthracene oxidation Slide 3

In the slide, all derivatives are drawn as arrows coming out of Anthracene (centre). Blue arrows point to the group that distinguishes each one.

DerivativeGroup(s) arrowed in the slide figure
AnthraceneParent compound (centre of the scheme)
AnthranolOH on the middle ring
AnthroneOne C=O (O) on the middle ring
AnthraquinoneTwo C=O (O, O) on the middle ring — one top, one bottom
OxanthroneC=O (O) on top + HO on the bottom of the middle ring
DianthroneTwo anthrone units joined together (dimer), each with its O
Quick Review
  • Aglycones = Anthracene derivatives → active constituents of plant cathartics/stimulant laxatives.
  • Oxidation-level forms: Anthraquinone, Anthrone, Oxanthrone, Anthranol + dimeric dianthrone (in some cases).

Anthraquinone glycosides Slide 4

  • These glycosides on hydrolysis , yield aglycones which are di, tri, or tetra hydroxyl anthraquinones or modifications of these compounds.
  • KEY Without the sugar moieties, free anthraquinone exhibit little therapeutic activity. They mostly exist as glycosides.
  • The sugar is essential because it serves to transport the aglycone to the site of action in the large intestine where it acts as a stimulant laxative to relief constipation (laxative).

Pharmacological action Slide 5

Oral administration→ Anthraquinone glucosides reach the colon→ Hydrolyzed by enzymes of the micro flora→ Pharmacologically active aglycones→ Effect in 8 -12 hrs
  • How they workStimulant laxatives exert their effect by increasing the tone of the smooth muscles in the wall of the colon and stimulate the secretion of water and electrolytes into the large intestines.
  • Activation & onsetAfter the oral administration, the anthraquinone glucosides are hydrolyzed in the colon by the action of enzymes of the micro flora, to the pharmacologically active aglycones which usually produce their effect in 8 -12 hrs.
  • IndicationsThese agents are indicated for constipation in/patient who do not respond to milder drugs and for bowel evacuation before investigational procedure or surgery.
  • ⚠ CAUTION Stimulant laxative are habit forming so the long-term use may result in laxative dependence and loss of normal bowel function.
  • ComparisonAnthranol and anthrone glycosides cause a more irritant and gripping laxative effect than anthraquinone laxatives .
Quick Review
  • Aglycones = di-, tri- or tetra-hydroxyl anthraquinones (or modifications).
  • Free anthraquinone → little activity; the sugar transports the aglycone to the large intestine.
  • Colon micro-flora enzymes release the active aglycone → effect in 8 -12 hrs.
  • Habit forming → laxative dependence. Anthranol / anthrone glycosides = more irritant & gripping.

Quick Review
  • Anthrone → oxanthrone → anthraquinone (emodin) = oxidation steps.
  • Anthrone → dianthrone = oxidation; anthrone ⇅ anthranol = labelled reduction.

Anthraquinone aglycons Slide 7

Aloe emodin · Rhien · Chrysophanol — all three are Anthraquinone. In the figure they share OH at 1 and 8 and two C=O; the blue arrow marks the group at position 3, which is what tells them apart.

AglyconTypeGroup at position 3 (arrowed)
Aloe emodinAnthraquinoneCH2OH
RhienAnthraquinoneCOOH
ChrysophanolAnthraquinoneCH3

Anthraquinone glycosides — Aloins :(C-glycoside) Slide 8

AloinTypeSide chainSugar (arrowed)
BarbaloinAnthrone C- glycosideCH2OHGl bonded to the middle-ring carbon, with H
ChrysaloinAnthrone C- glycosideCH3Gl bonded to the middle-ring carbon, with H

Link forward: Barbaloin → Aloe-emodin and Chrysaloin → Chrysophanol by oxidative hydrolysis (Unit 7, Cascara).

Quick Review
  • Position 3: Aloe emodin = CH2OH · Rhien = COOH · Chrysophanol = CH3.
  • Aloins (Barbaloin, Chrysaloin) are anthrone C-glycosides.
  • The biosynthetic pathway starts with shikimic acid which forms 1-naphthol.
  • This last compound undergoes condensation with IPP (isopentenyl pyrophosphate) followed by cyclization to produce anthraquinone nucleus.
Shikimic acid→ 1-naphthol+ IPP from mevalonic acid pathway→ Intermediate→ Cyclization Anthraquinone nucleus
Quick Review
  • Two inputs: 1-naphthol (from shikimic acid) + IPP (from the mevalonic acid pathway).
  • Condensation → intermediate → cyclization → anthraquinone nucleus.
SourceSenna or senna leaves consists of dried leaflets of cassia acutifolia or cassia angustifolia
FamilyF:leguminoseae
Usescathartic laxative.
Dose12mg-15mg tab once daily (can be divided for every 12hr.)

The main constituents Slide 12

Is the dimeric glycosides :Sennoside A and Sennoside B (major content) while Sennoside C and Sennoside D (minor content). Both of which optical isomers.

Constituents — Sennoside A/B/C/D Slide 13

These contain two O-glycosides (dianthrone)

SennosideContentAnthronesIsomerism
A and Bmajor contenthas two identical anthrone (homo dianthrone: 2 rhien)they are optical isomers
C and Dminor contenthave different anthrones (hetero anthrones: rhien+aloe emodin)they are optical isomers

KEY The c-c linkage between the di-anthrones is difficult to be cleaved they are resistant to hydrolysis so we can use oxidative hydrolysis using ferric chloride to release the free anthraquinone rhein or aloe-emodin.

⚠ CAUTION Habitual constipation Slide 14

Senna and other stimulant laxatives should not be used more than a week since they can cause loss of muscular tone in the large intestines causing habitual constipation making things worse for constipation patients.

Dose: 12mg-15mg tab once daily (can be divided for every 12hr.)

Quick Review
  • Dried leaflets of cassia acutifolia / cassia angustifolia, leguminoseae.
  • Sennosides A/B (major, 2 rhien) · C/D (minor, rhien + aloe emodin) — dimeric, optical isomers.
  • C–C link resists hydrolysis → oxidative hydrolysis with ferric chloride.
  • Not more than a week · 12mg-15mg once daily.
SourceIs the dried bark of Rhamnus purshiana
FamilyF: Rhamnaceae.
Ageingat least one year before use
Usesconstipation and colon cleansing

Drug & preparation Slide 15

  • It should be aged for at least one year prior to use in medicinal preparations ( to lose its gripping properties when oxidized with storage).
  • KEY B. P. specified that the collection must be made at least one year before the bark is used since the fresh bark contains an emetic principle.
  • The plant is being used to treat constipation and colon cleansing where it can restore the natural tone of the colon (in cases of habitual constipation).

Cascara constituents Slides 16–17

CascarosidesGlycoside typeR
A/BO- and C- glycosidesCH2OH
C/DO- and C- glycosidesCH3
  • Thus, the glycosidic linkage binds with an oxygen while the other binds with a carbon atom (disaccharide anthrone glycoside)
  • The difference is due to the stereochemistry of the carbon at the glycosidic linkage.

Slide 16 figure: two structures, each with Glucose—O on the left ring (arrowed) and Glucose on the middle-ring carbon with H (arrowed); they differ only in the wedge/hash orientation of H and Glucose at that carbon.

Slide 17 — Difference in the side chain between Cascarosides A/B and Cascarosides C/D: A and B carry the CH2–OH side chain, C and D carry CH3 (green arrows); A vs B (and C vs D) differ in the orientation of H and Glc at the middle-ring carbon (red box).

Quick Review
  • Dried bark of Rhamnus purshiana (Rhamnaceae); aged ≥ 1 year (fresh bark = emetic; loses gripping properties on storage).
  • Cascarosides = O- and C- glycosides (disaccharide anthrone glycoside): A/B R = CH2OH; C/D R = CH3.
  • A/B → Barbaloin → Aloe-emodin; C/D → Chrysaloin → Chrysophanol.
SourceAloe is the dried juice of aloe perri or aloe barbadensis
FamilyF:liliacea.
Speciesabout 50 species of aloe are known

There are about 50 species of aloe are known where the active constituents vary qualitatively and quantitatively .

Aloe uses Slide 22

  1. As a cathartic laxative by acting on the large intestine.
  2. The fresh juice has been used in the treatment of burns & other skin irritations.
  3. The extracted gel could be blended with a special base to form an ointment recommended for the treatment of sunburn, deep thermal burns & radiation burns.
  4. It affords relief from pain & itching & ulceration, thus preventing change into malignancy

Aloe – constituents Slide 23

  • Aloe contains the C- glycoside : Barbaloin>>>> aloe- emodin present either as free aglycon or as combined.
  • The moisturizing effect of aloe is due to the carbohydrate content like pectin and glucomannan
Quick Review
  • Dried juice of aloe perri / aloe barbadensis (liliacea); ~50 species.
  • 4 uses: laxative · burns & skin irritation (fresh juice) · gel ointment for sunburn / thermal / radiation burns · relief of pain, itching, ulceration.
  • Barbaloin (C-glycoside) → aloe-emodin; moisturizing = pectin & glucomannan.
SourceIs the dried rhizomes and root of Rheum officinal
FamilyF:polygonaceae
UsesAs a cathartic laxative and it has astringent properties.

Constituents

  • Chrysophanol
  • Rhien and rhein anthrone
  • Aloe emodin

⚠ CAUTION Aloe and rhubarb are less widely used than senna and cascara due to stronger gripping effect.
